title: Distinguish module exports from supported package entry points
applies_when: A JavaScript or TypeScript helper is declared export function and a candidate assumes that package users can call it, especially in a native-binding package with explicit package.json exports.
lesson: Trace the published entry's re-exports and the package export map before building a native runtime to reproduce an isolated helper defect. A module-level export alone does not establish a supported package API. In LanceDB ca275b6, arrow.ts declares several incorrectly copied type guards, but index.ts re-exports only selected Arrow helpers and the package export map does not expose the Arrow submodule. Treat the guard discrepancy as a source defect with unproven user reachability, not automatically as a user-facing regression. Check internal callers separately; if neither a supported entry nor a real caller reaches it, defer a bugfix PR pending maintainer interest or new caller evidence.
avoid_when: Do not reject genuinely public helpers merely because no internal caller exists. An export map does not prove that all aliases, generated bundles, older releases or consumer environments hide a module. This case is source-level inspection of one revision, not native package execution or proof of no possible use. A direct internal-module test alone would not qualify the public API allegation.

evidence.note: Several guard declarations use Utf8, and isUnion uses Struct. This supports a local source discrepancy only; it does not establish supported API exposure or native behavior.
The package entry selectively re-exports makeArrowTable, makeJsonField, MakeArrowTableOptions, Data and VectorColumnOptions, not the affected guards.
The exports map exposes the main entry and three embedding entries, not an Arrow subpath. Source manifest evidence, not an installed-package resolution test.
